newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council President raps Burundi on rights probe.
newsitem.headline: UN Council President raps Burundi on rights probe.

text.p: The president of the U.N. Security Council on Thursday said members were dismayed by fighting in Burundi, the summary execution of prisoners and the barring of a U.N. human rights investigator.
Following the lead of Congo leader Laurent Kabila's Congo, Burundi recently demanded the designated U.N. human rights investigator, Paulo Sergio Pinheiro of Brazil, be replaced.
The United Nations organized a new team for the Congo but refused to set a precedent and do the same for Burundi.

"It really is not acceptable that he should be prevented from going about its mandate in Burundi and not be allowed freedom of movement and freedom of access and we want to underline the importance of that," said British Ambassador Sir John Weston, the current council president.

He told reporters after closed-door council consultations, that members hoped all factions would attend peace talks in Arusha, Tanzania, on August 5, led by former Tanzanian President Julius Nyrere and U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun.

But he said all concerned should "do whatever they can to contribute to a climate of trust and not to increase a climate of distrust," particularly regarding the need for "a fair and impartial judicial system and due process of law."
Burundi's government on July 31 executed six prisoners accused of genocide in 1993 massacres amid complaints they did not receive a fair trail before their July 31 hangings.

More than 250,000 people have been killed in Burundi in massacres and civil war between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels since the assassination of Burundi's firt Hutu president in October 1993.

Most recently reports said that 600 Hutu civilians were killed by rival Hutu rebels, with one group accusing another of collaborating with Burundi's Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya by agreeing to peace talks.
Buyoya, who seized power a year ago, has also ordered 200,000 civilians, mainly Hutus, into relocation campas guarded by the army, a situation harsely criticized by human rights groups.
